Canada readies retaliatory tariffs as Trump ramps up trade threats
Canada will announce retaliatory tariffs after trade talks with the Trump administration collapsed. The clash has widened into a fight over sovereignty, jobs and the future of key industries.
Canada is set to announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday, according to an official familiar with the plans, in a sharp escalation of a trade fight that has worsened since talks with the Trump administration collapsed. Prime Minister Mark Carney said Ottawa may no longer match US tariffs dollar for dollar and could instead use more targeted measures to protect Canadian workers and businesses.
US President Donald Trump intensified the dispute on Monday, telling Canadian leaders to "fall in line" or face consequences "far WORSE" than the tariffs already imposed. He also threatened new 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel, prompting Carney to accuse Washington of trying to subordinate Canada and dismantle major Canadian industries.
The official who spoke about Canada's tariff plans did so on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss them publicly. The latest confrontation follows Carney's decision late on Friday to walk away from trade negotiations with the Trump administration, after which Trump threatened 50 per cent tariffs on about USD 20 billion worth of Canadian goods the next day.
Carney said, "An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States" is "not something we're going to accept". He was even blunter in French, saying, "We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminium. That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal." He also questioned Washington's reliability, saying Canada was finding reliable partners "everywhere in the world, except in the United States. Except in the United States. And Russia."
Trump returned to the offensive on Monday by warning that further tariffs would hit Canada's auto industry from next year. "Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years," he wrote on social media, while criticising what he called the country's "ridiculously high tariffs" on American farmers. Carney said the US proposals on the auto sector would gradually dismantle Canadian production, adding, "This is the most successful automotive partnership in history," in reference to the deeply integrated Canada-US industry.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford also struck a defiant note in an interview with The Associated Press, saying Trump had underestimated Canadians' willingness to bear economic pain rather than give in. "We're all in," Ford said. "Up here, we're at a fever pitch; everyone's in for an economic war. They know they're going to have to sacrifice." After Trump called him "the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford" and again referred to the prime minister as "Governor Carney", Ford replied, "If you think an insult from him hurts me? Well, bring it on, buddy, I'm ready." Although Ford is a Progressive Conservative and Carney is a Liberal, both have underlined a broad political unity in Canada over the dispute.
Ford said "everything is on the table" if the fight worsens, including cutting off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario. He said Canada should also consider stronger retaliation if Trump continues targeting Canadian industries, including oil and potash, while Ontario could raise electricity prices or stop sending power south. "We power 1.5 million homes and businesses," Ford said. "Everything's on the table. I'll do whatever it takes." Critical minerals have become increasingly important for US national security and manufacturing, and the Pentagon has sought more secure supplies for military aircraft, missiles, munitions and electronics as Washington tries to reduce reliance on China. Ford has used electricity as leverage before: in an earlier phase of the dispute, Ontario imposed a 25 per cent surcharge on electricity exported to Michigan, Minnesota and New York before both sides stepped back.
The auto industry has now become a central battleground. Ford accused Trump of trying not just to secure a better trade deal but to hollow out Canadian industries and shift production south. He said Trump wanted to make Canada a vassal state, adding, "He wants to bleed out every single sector and bring them down to the US." The sector is especially important to Ontario, where plants and suppliers are tightly linked with factories in Michigan and other US states, with parts crossing the border multiple times during production. Automakers including Ford, General Motors and Stellantis run major assembly plants in Ontario, and the wider supply chain supports tens of thousands of jobs. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Monday that "the only reason Canada has auto production in the first place" was the 1960s Auto Pact, under which Canada used access to its market to encourage vehicle production north of the border.
Ford also said he had opposed the preliminary deal Carney had been considering before Canada broke off negotiations, and that he was not prepared to restore American liquor to Ontario shop shelves as part of any agreement. "I wasn't going to put the booze back on the shelves," Ford said. "I was ready to go out there and call a press conference ... and say I'm not buckling over." He said he understood that Washington had sought language late in the talks that would have limited Canada's ability to negotiate trade agreements with other countries without US approval, a demand Carney has called unacceptable and a matter of Canadian sovereignty. Carney also said the dispute had exposed a deeper divide over language and culture, with protections for French and Canadian culture seen by Washington as trade irritants but treated in Canada as fundamental rights.
With Canada preparing fresh tariffs and the US threatening more duties, the dispute has widened beyond trade to questions of industry, sovereignty and political resolve. Summing up the mood in Canada, Ford said of Trump, "Who does he think he is? You gotta be kidding."
With PTI Inputs

Canada poised to strike back at Trump with retaliatory tariffs
sources.text:
Canada is expected to announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday after President Donald Trump said he would reimplement 50 percent tariffs on imports from Canada into the United States, an official familiar with the plan told the Associated Press.
In a post on Truth Social, following back-and-forth over the weekend around tariffs, Trump said "ridiculously high" tariffs imposed by Canada on American farmers and farm products had "made life impossible" for farmers who he called "great American patriots."
New 50 percent tariffs will be imposed on cars, trucks, automotive parts, and steel from January 1, 2027, Trump said.
"Canada will be treated like a State no longer!" the president posted. "On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with. They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED U.S.!"
Over the weekend, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada was "at war" with the U.S. over trade.
"On a broader scale, any trade conflict between Canada and the United States is likely to have a bigger impact on the Canadian economy, given the share of trade that accounts for each country's GDP," Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a policy analyst at the libertarian Cato Institute, told Newsweek.
The escalation from Trump was backed by messaging from the White House, with spokesperson Kush Desai telling Newsweek that American workers, businesses, and farmers had been undermined by unfair trade practices for decades.
"Canada tore up an incredibly generous and fair trade deal with the Trump administration to instead demand unrestricted access to the American economy while boxing American exports out of its market," Desai said Monday. "President Trump will never waver from putting Americans and America First."
Speaking to reporters Monday, Carney said the goal for those negotiations had always been about getting the best deal for Canadians.
"While we did make some progress in recent weeks, in the end, that momentum reversed and we could not accept what the U.S. had offered, nor could we give what they asked," Carney said. "And by standing up for our values and focusing on what we can control, we will build."
Carney's office pointed to his news conference when reached for comment by Newsweek.
What Trump's Threat Means for the North American Auto Industry
Trump's latest threat targets one of the most integrated supply chains in the world. For decades, the U.S. and Canadian auto industries have functioned as a single manufacturing system under different agreements.
Components routinely cross the border multiple times before a vehicle reaches a dealership. Industry groups and trade researchers say that imposing 50 percent tariffs on Canadian-built vehicles, parts and steel would not simply affect Canadian manufacturers. It would raise costs throughout the North American production chain, including for U.S. plants that rely on Canadian inputs.
While Trump framed the relationship as one-sided, recent research suggests the automotive trade relationship is more balanced than it appears when looking only at finished vehicles. The United States runs a substantial surplus in auto parts trade with Canada, and the two countries' automotive sectors are deeply intertwined.
Analysts at the Lawrence Centre for Policy and Management describe the relationship as one of "integration and mutual dependence" rather than a simple exporter-importer dynamic.
Cars, Trucks Targeted With New Tariffs
Canada's auto industry remains deeply intertwined with the U.S., with millions of vehicles and parts crossing the border each year. Many Canadian assembly plants produce vehicles specifically for the U.S. market.
While many consumers think of Detroit as the center of North American auto manufacturing, several popular vehicles sold in the U.S. are assembled in Ontario before being imported south. Industry data shows Canada remains a major exporter of passenger vehicles to the U.S. market, particularly SUVs, minivans, and some pickup trucks.
Major vehicles assembled in Canada and imported into the U.S. include:
- Toyota RAV4 (Woodstock, Ontario)
- Toyota RAV4 Hybrid (Woodstock, Ontario)
- Lexus NX and NX Hybrid (Cambridge, Ontario)
- Honda CR-V (Alliston, Ontario production)
- Chrysler Pacifica and Pacifica Plug-In Hybrid (Windsor, Ontario)
- Chrysler Voyager (Windsor, Ontario)
- Dodge Charger (Windsor, Ontario)
- Chevrolet Silverado HD (Oshawa, Ontario)
- Some Chevrolet Silverado 1500 models (Oshawa, Ontario)
The cross-border supply chain means that even vehicles assembled in Canada often contain significant U.S.-made components, while many vehicles assembled in the U.S. rely on Canadian parts.
US-Canada Trade: Who Needs Who More?
Trump argued that Canada does "95 percent" of its business with the United States while the reverse is not true. Canada is unquestionably more dependent on the U.S. market than the U.S. is on Canada. However, recent trade data suggest the 95 percent figure significantly overstates current trade dependence.
Statistics Canada and private-sector analyses show roughly 72 percent of Canadian goods exports crossed its southern border in 2025, down from about 76 percent a year earlier as Canadian businesses sought alternative markets amid trade tensions. Even so, the U.S. remains by far Canada's largest trading partner.
At the same time, Canada remains one of America's most important economic partners. According to U.S. trade data, Canada was the United States' second-largest overall trading partner in 2025, accounting for nearly $880 billion in two-way trade. The United States imported approximately $454 billion in goods and services from Canada and exported roughly $426 billion.
Obregon told Newsweek that the robustness of Canadian-American supply chains goes beyond topline GDP data.
"A tariff back-and-forth can therefore hurt American companies that rely on these production networks," he said, adding that, "Tariffs will likely have a disproportionate impact on states and communities along our shared border, including Michigan (e.g., auto industry in Detroit-Windsor), Maine (e.g., lobster industry that processes catch in New Brunswick), and New York.
"Moreover, there are 13 states for which Canada is the destination for more than one-quarter of their respective total exports; Canadian retaliation could hurt businesses and communities in these states."
Maine Republican Senator Susan Collins, speaking to reporters Monday, said she felt imposing tariffs on Canada was "a mistake," in part because of her state's mutually beneficial relationship.
"We produce a lot in Maine. Our blueberries, our lobster, our lumber, that is process across the border," Collins said. "If that comes back with a huge tariff on it, perhaps as much as 50 percent, that increases the cost of eating, building homes, and merchanting out best-known products."
What Are the Key U.S.-Canada Trade Disputes Right Now?
This latest threat comes after months of deteriorating trade relations between the two countries.
Recent negotiations aimed at reducing existing tariffs on steel, aluminum and automobiles collapsed last week, with both governments publicly blaming the other. Canada has announced retaliatory tariffs, while the Trump administration has accused Ottawa of seeking additional concessions during negotiations.
The broader dispute now stretches across several sectors:
- Automobiles: The Trump administration says vehicle production should be shifted back to the U.S.; Canada argues integrated supply chains make that unrealistic.
- Steel and Aluminum: These industries have been subject to repeated tariff battles and were central to the failed negotiations.

American Action Forum President Douglas Holtz-Eakin's told Newsweek that "tit-for-tat tariffs" from both sides were a dangerous development.
"The silver lining is that these new tariffs are deferred until January; perhaps in the interim a trading relationship to which both sides will adhere may emerge," Holtz-Eakin said. "And, perhaps these tariffs will be mitigated by exempting USMCA-compliant goods, as has been done for Mexico and Canada in the past."
Obregon said that the escalation Monday casts more uncertainty over how an extension of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) could be achieved.
"This is the largest downside of this dispute and any further escalation, as businesses that rely on an integrated North America may be hesitant to make long-term investments without the security that the agreement—which, for now, remains in effect for 10 more years—will be extended for a longer period," Obregon said.

Canada Response to Trump Tariffs Set for Tuesday Announcement
Ottawa prepares to unveil retaliatory measures as the trade fight with Washington deepens
Canada vs US – (Special Correspondent/Web Desk) – Canada’s response to Trump tariffs will be revealed on Tuesday, as officials in Ottawa get ready to unveil their next move in a fast-growing trade fight with the United States. The announcement comes just days after Washington’s new 50 percent tariffs on select Canadian goods took effect.
The Canadian government confirmed that finance, industry, and labour ministers will hold a press conference to explain the country’s plan. Officials called the situation “challenging times” and said new steps will be introduced to support workers and businesses across the country.
The tension began building last week when talks between Canada and the US failed to produce a deal. Despite weeks of negotiations, both sides could not agree on terms, and the new tariffs kicked in over the weekend.
Adding more pressure, Trump said Monday that auto tariffs on Canadian vehicles would double next year, rising to 50 percent. Right now, non-US content in Canadian autos faces a 25 percent tariff, while steel imports into the US already carry a 50 percent duty.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney turned down what he described as a “bad deal” from Washington. In turn, he announced retaliatory tariffs that will start on September 8. These new measures will target American steel and dairy products, along with farm equipment, paper goods, and electronics.
Carney explained that Canada’s goal throughout the talks was never to settle for just any agreement. He said the country wanted a fair deal, not one rushed for the sake of a deadline.
He also revealed that American negotiators pushed for terms that could have hurt major Canadian industries, including automotive, steel, and aluminum. According to Carney, this was one of the biggest reasons Canada chose to walk away.
Beyond trade numbers, Carney said the US side also raised concerns about Canada’s trade ties with other nations. He added that American officials even questioned protections for the French language and culture in Quebec, calling the demands unacceptable.
Meanwhile, US Vice President JD Vance placed blame on Canada, saying the country made “unreasonable last-minute demands” during the negotiations.
The stakes are high for both nations. The US remains Canada’s largest trading partner, receiving about 70 percent of all Canadian exports. On the flip side, Canada ranks as the second-largest goods trading partner for the US this year.
Public opinion in Canada appears to back Carney’s tough stance. A recent survey by the Angus Reid Institute found that three out of four Canadians support the decision to step away from the trade talks. Still, many remain worried, as two in five Canadians fear the dispute could put their jobs at risk.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford also weighed in, strongly criticizing Trump’s tariff threats on the auto sector. Ford has warned that an electricity surcharge remains a possible response if tensions continue to rise.

The United States imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian products, and Canada immediately said it would retaliate after last-ditch negotiations failed to resolve the latest strain in relations between the two longtime allies, Paul Wiseman and Rob Gillies reported for The Associated Press (AP).
The new tariffs will affect about 5% of Canada's annual exports to the United States, including products ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors.
“Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said.
The retaliation escalates the trade conflict and raises fresh questions about the future of the North American trade framework between the United States, Canada and Mexico, which is important to industries across all three countries.
Canada had sought concessions from Washington on tariffs affecting steel, aluminum, vehicles and lumber, but the United States was unwilling to provide the concessions Ottawa wanted, a senior Trump administration official said.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Canada had declined to finalize a trade deal under terms the United States believed had been agreed upon earlier in the week.
He accused Canada of making new demands and backing away from previous commitments.
Carney blamed Washington for the breakdown, saying last-minute changes to the US proposal were unfair and uneconomic. He said he had suspended negotiations and instructed Canada's negotiating team to return to Ottawa.
He also said his government would announce additional support for Canadian workers and businesses.

The trade war between the United States and Canada has reached a critical flashpoint following the collapse of high-stakes negotiations with the Trump administration. While the United States continues to maintain an aggressive posture, Canada is prepared to announce significant and stringent retaliatory tariffs against its southern neighbor on Tuesday. This move marks a definitive escalation in the economic tensions that have gripped North American trade relations since President Donald Trump signaled his intent to impose heavy duties on Canadian goods.
The Failure of Washington Negotiations
The current crisis stems from the failure of diplomatic efforts to resolve trade disputes. Despite high-level discussions aimed at averting a full-scale trade war, the talks yielded no positive results. The final attempt at a resolution took place late Friday night in Washington, where representatives from both nations engaged in intense dialogue. However, these negotiations ended in a stalemate, leaving both countries on the brink of a significant economic confrontation. As a result, Canada has decided to move forward with its own set of tariffs to protect its national interests.
Mark Carney Asserts Canadian Sovereignty
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has issued a stern response to the pressure from Washington. In a sharp critique of the US administration's approach, Carney stated that the United States is attempting to treat Canada as a subsidiary rather than a sovereign partner, while he emphasized that such a dynamic is entirely unacceptable, declaring that Canada isn't a slave to the United States. Carney clarified that Canada's strategy will now evolve beyond a simple dollar-for-dollar retaliatory policy. Instead, the government will implement targeted measures specifically designed to safeguard Canadian workers and businesses from external economic aggression.
Trump's Tariff Threats and Economic Consequences
President Donald Trump has further intensified the conflict by directly challenging the Canadian leadership. Trump has warned the current Canadian administration to fall in line, cautioning that failure to do so would result in much worse consequences than the currently proposed tariffs. The President has threatened to impose a new 50 percent tariff on Canadian vehicles, auto parts, and steel, with the total value of affected goods estimated at approximately 20 billion dollars. These tariffs are scheduled to take effect next year, posing a severe threat to Canada's industrial sector.
Unacceptable Conditions and Trade Credibility
Prime Minister Carney explained that the conditions presented by Donald Trump were fundamentally unacceptable, while he described the terms as economically unjust and contrary to Canada's national interests. Also, Carney argued that these conditions undermined the credibility of any potential trade agreement and severely limited Canada's ability to negotiate future trade deals, while however, Carney did offer a path toward de-escalation, stating that if the United States Importantly reduces its tariffs, Canada would be willing to remove its retaliatory duties on American aluminum, steel, and motor vehicles.
Political Unity and Personal Attacks
The trade dispute has also taken a personal turn, with President Trump utilizing social media to accuse Canada of fleecing the United States for years. He specifically targeted Canadian tariffs on American farmers. In response, Ontario Premier Doug Ford, a Progressive Conservative, has joined forces with Liberal Prime Minister Carney, showcasing a rare moment of political unity in Canada. Ford remarked that Trump has underestimated the resolve of the Canadian people to endure economic hardship rather than succumb to American pressure. He stated that the country is fully prepared for this economic war.
Escalating Rhetoric and Personal Insults
The conflict has devolved into personal insults, with Trump attacking Doug Ford on social media. The President referred to Ford as the less charismatic and less intelligent brother of the late Rob Ford, labeling him as overall ineffective. Trump also continued to mock the Prime Minister by referring to him as Governor Carney. Doug Ford dismissed these insults, challenging the President by stating that if he thought personal attacks would hurt him, he was mistaken, while ford concluded by expressing his readiness for the confrontation, signaling that Canada won't back down from the impending trade battle.
